extracted.intended_audience: IP lawyers, judges, scholars, and practitioners handling patent/trademark damages under Korean law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical criteria for presuming, rebutting, and calculating damages based on an infringer's profit under Korean Patent, Trademark, and Unfair Competition law, with illustrative precedents and calculation methods. Focuses on when damages are presumed, required proofs, and concrete methods courts accept to compute profits/damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of damages from infringer's profit
rubrics_metrics.description: When an infringer earns a profit due to the infringement act, that profit is presumed to be the amount of damages the right holder has sustained (e.g., Article 37(2) former Trademark Act; Article 128, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (OK Powdered Wasabi Case) holds that the trademark owner needs to prove the infringer's profit but does not have to prove a causal relationship between the infringement and occurrence of damages when the statutory presumption applies. For patents, Article 128(4) similarly presumes causation when the provision for presuming amount of damages is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of causal relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statute presumes the amount of damages based on infringer's profit, a causal relationship between the infringement act and the occurrence of damages is also presumed by the provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that without presuming causation, the presumption of amount would be ineffective; courts have interpreted Article 128, Paragraph 4 to carry this presumption. See discussion of the Patent Act and related precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right holder's working/use as application requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a right holder must 'work' (use/manufacture/sell) the patented invention or registered trademark to invoke the presumption or claim damages is a key application requirement and differs by statute and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seoul District Court (Textile Machine Thread Storing...) held that 'working' is not an active requirement for Article 128(2) of the Patent Act. By contrast, trademark case law (e.g., Supreme Court decisions cited) often finds no damages where the trademark owner did not perform business activities using the mark in the territory. Article 111 (amended Trademark Act) requires use of a registered trademark as a requirement for claiming statutory damages up to 50M won.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal of the presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption that infringer's profit equals right holder's damages can be rebutted when it is proved that the actual amount of damages of the right holder is less than the presumed amount due to special circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize that infringer profit may derive from many non-infringement sources (capital, sales ability, advertising, product quality, technology, trademark, design, company credit, sales system, characters). Listing such sources does not automatically rebut the presumption; the infringer bears the burden of proof to show special circumstances and that actual damages are smaller than presumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: The infringer has the burden to prove that profits were earned from sources other than the infringement (special circumstances) to rebut the statutory presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Cheogajip Fried Chicken Case; SUNX Case) emphasizes that while various factors may contribute to infringer profit, the presumption is not rebutted simply by asserting those factors; the infringer must prove them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning/scope of 'profit' for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'profit' referred to in statutory provisions means all profit the infringer obtains by execution of the patented invention (or infringing use) without permission; it has no special limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photoconductive Drum Case explains profit includes domestic sales, exports, and profits from competitive effects; however, the statutory provision is a method for evaluating damages, not applicable where patentee has no losses despite infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical approaches to scope of deductible costs (net/gross/marginal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three competing theories define what expenses to deduct from infringer sales to reach 'profit': (A) Net benefit theory deducts all expenses (fixed+variable); (B) Gross benefit theory deducts manufacturing/selling costs and overhead but not general administrative expenses; (C) Marginal profit theory deducts only production-dependent variable costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents vary: Cheogajip appears to follow the marginal profit theory (deduct additionally incurred expenses). Choice of theory affects whether fixed/general administrative expenses are deductible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's obligation to use a reasonable calculation method
rubrics_metrics.description: When exact expense figures are not submitted, courts shall employ a reasonable method to estimate items constituting the defendant's expenses; the method used must retain rationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photosensitive Drum Case: if no evidence allows precise calculation, court should estimate items reasonably rather than refuse damages; the chosen method must be rational and based on the gist of arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: proportionate deduction using gross profit and expense ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate gross profit on sales attributable to the infringing product by ratio of related-sales to gross sales, then deduct selling and general administrative expenses proportionally (except for depreciation and executive salaries that are regular regardless of these sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seoul Central District Court (2002Gahap30683) used formula: gross profit on sales * (sales related to infringing product / gross sales) - (selling & G&A expenses - fixed costs) * (sales related / gross sales). This approach apportions company-wide figures to the infringing product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: utilize a standard income rate (industry simple-expense rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: When defendant-specific expense data are unavailable, courts may apply a standard income rate derived from National Tax Service simple expense rates or industry standard income rates to estimate profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (e.g., Suwon and Seoul examples) accept using the Income Tax Act estimation method: use the industry 'standard income rate' (1 - simple expense rate) as a proxy for operating income rate, and multiply acknowledged sales by that rate to compute damages (Article 128(5) applied where facts are difficult to prove).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: estimate income using Income Tax Act analog
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate infringer profit as: Sales of infringed product - main expenses related to infringed product (purchase price + rent + personnel) - (sales * basic expense rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suwon District Court (2008Gahap23845) described this estimation method when direct accounting evidence is insufficient; it analogizes to tax simple-expense approaches and permits deduction of main direct costs plus a basic expense rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: use right holder's net profit ratio to estimate infringer profit
rubrics_metrics.description: In some trademark precedents the amount of profit that the infringer has earned may be calculated by multiplying the infringer's sales amount by the net profit ratio of the trademark owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SUNX Case: courts have used the right holder's net profit ratio to estimate infringer profit when direct data for the infringer are lacking; this produces an estimated net profit amount presumed to be damages absent special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption where no damages occurred (non-use/no reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringer may be exempted from compensation if it is proved that no damages occurred to the right holder—for example, where the trademark owner did not use the registered trademark in the relevant territory and no business credit or customer attraction was reflected in the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and district court decisions (e.g., IAS Case, NAFS-III Case) find no damage where trademark was not used and no reputation established; courts examine whether the mark performed source-identification or promotional functions, or had past use establishing credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 128(5) / judicial discretion for reasonable damages
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is extremely difficult to prove particular facts needed to calculate damages, the court may recognize reasonable damages based on the gist of arguments and the evidence examination (statutory safety valve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts invoke Paragraph 5 (Patent Act) to admit reasonable damages where plaintiffs cannot prove detailed expense data; judges may apply estimation methods (standard income, operating income rate, etc.) to reach a reasonable figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to sales data reliability and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When competing sales data sources exist (e.g., HIRA drug bills vs. private market estimates), courts evaluate objectivity, sampling, and scope to determine which sales data to rely on for calculating infringer sales and thus profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pharmaceutical cases, courts favored HIRA drug-bill data over private estimation (UBcare) due to objectivity and comprehensive coverage. The selection of sales data materially affects the profit computation and courts will explain reasoning.
